name: CASSOULET PET Suite
eli5: A flight simulator for PET scanners: put in a virtual patient, get the image a real scanner would make.
summary: Compositional Anthropomorphic Spatial Synthesizer for ground-truth Lesion Export: an analytical PET/CT simulator that inserts uniform, heterogeneous and patient-shaped lesions into phantom or patient data on modern scanners.

more.problem: Vendor simulators are closed and couldn't insert heterogeneous or necrotic lesions, or patient-derived shapes, on the scanners used in the thesis.
approach: Core architecture follows PETSTEP; noise-factor count calibration and crystal normalisation inspired by SMART-PET
Insertion uses the same fractional-mask logic as GE DUETTO; CT simulated in the image domain
Scanner models of GE Discovery MI 5-ring, GE OMNI Legend 32 cm and Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra, from published NEMA and open data
Physics v2 adds depth-of-interaction sub-LORs, TOF single-scatter simulation, BSREM/OSEM and DICOM export, running on GPUs
outcome: Reproduced heterogeneous-insert trends against physical experiments in the PhD
More than 150 dated studies in October 2026; multicentre manuscripts in preparation

headline: An analytical PET/CT simulator that inserts uniform, heterogeneous and patient-shaped lesions into phantom or patient data, modelled on three current clinical scanners.

brief.problem: Vendor simulators are closed and could not insert heterogeneous or necrotic lesions, or patient-derived shapes, on the scanners in use.
brief.built: Two connected modules. A design module builds the lesion truth object (draw or import a mask, upsample it to sub-voxels, split rim, core and hotspots, assign uptake or time-activity curves, export to simulation or an STL for printing). A GPU simulator projects background and lesion separately, adds calibrated noise, mixes the data and reconstructs it (BSREM/OSEM) with DICOM export, for the GE Discovery MI, GE OMNI Legend and Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra.
brief.result: Reproduced the heterogeneous-insert trends measured in physical experiments, with similar CoV and Gini-index trends across nine configurations. On eight patient-derived lesion geometries the simulated and printed-phantom results were broadly similar, with one outlier. More than 150 dated studies by October 2026; multicentre manuscripts in preparation.

role: Designed and wrote the simulator, then ran the thesis studies with it: cross-validation against 3D-printed porous phantoms on the GE Discovery MI and OMNI Legend, and a feasibility study on eight patient-derived lesion geometries.
team: PhD at IUCT Oncopole, Université de Toulouse. Related papers with Q. Maronnier, J. A. Kennedy and O. Caselles.

name: MuPET: Multiphysics PET
eli5: Use the physics of how things spread through tissue to make realistic, fully known fake PET scans.
summary: Couples computational mass-transport physics with PET simulation to generate synthetic PET data whose ground-truth activity is known.
abstract:
Purpose: Robust positron emission tomography (PET) research increasingly requires reliable ground-truth activity distributions, yet clinical data and physical phantoms cannot provide them fully. This work introduces MuPET (multiphysics PET), a computational framework that bridges mass-transport physics simulation with image domain noise modeling to generate realistic, synthetic PET images.

Methods: Tracer transport and radioactive decay within a custom phantom geometry were modeled via decay diffusion physics. The simulated activity concentrations were converted into PET equivalent count maps, followed by a pseudo-Poisson noise model calibrated to scanner-specific characteristics. MuPET generated images were compared with experimental PET acquisitions and a conventional synthetic lesion insertion pipeline. VOI (volume of interest) and ROI (region interest) data extraction was performed on all the data. The quantitative metrics included the recovery coefficient (RC), target contrast ratio (TCR), coefficient of variability (COV), and activity profile.

Results: The simulated effective activities matched the decay-corrected measurements within 0.4-1.2%, confirming high physics-model fidelity. The optimized noise model achieved COV values (3.9-4.0%) comparable to those of the acquisitions (3.8-3.9%). MuPET demonstrated strong agreement with the experimental profiles and quantitative metrics, with mean biases within 10% of the acquisition.

Conclusion: MuPET establishes a fast (approximately 15 min), physically grounded pipeline that combines transport modeling with PET image simulation, enabling generation of realistic datasets. This approach provides a practical foundation for future dynamic PET simulations.
headline: Synthetic PET images with a known ground truth, generated from tracer-transport physics in about 15 minutes and checked against real scanner acquisitions.

brief.problem: PET research needs ground-truth activity distributions that clinical data and physical phantoms cannot fully provide, and 3D-printed phantom designs are only tested after they have been printed and scanned.
brief.built: A multiphysics framework: tracer transport and radioactive decay (decay diffusion) are simulated inside a custom phantom geometry, the activity is converted to PET-equivalent count maps, and a pseudo-Poisson noise model calibrated to the scanner makes the images realistic. VOI and ROI analysis gives recovery coefficient, target contrast ratio, coefficient of variability and activity profiles.
brief.result: Simulated activities matched decay-corrected measurements within 0.4–1.2 %; image noise (COV 3.9–4.0 %) matched the acquisitions (3.8–3.9 %), with mean biases within 10 %.

role: First and corresponding author. The preprint compares MuPET images with experimental PET acquisitions of a 3D-printed phantom and with a conventional synthetic lesion insertion pipeline.
team: Nalla, Maronnier, Kennedy, Uppapalli, Caselles. IUCT and Oncopole Toulouse, Rambam Health Care Campus and Technion (Haifa), Mahindra University, Tachyons SAS.

name: Bench test for pulmonary valve implantation
context: M1 internship · Hôpital Marie Lannelongue (Groupe Hospitalier Paris Saint-Joseph)
eli5: A 3D-printed heart on a bench, so cardiologists can rehearse fitting a new valve before the real operation.
summary: Redesign of a surgical simulation bench test for percutaneous pulmonary valve implantation (PPVI) in congenital heart disease, advised by Dr Sébastien Hascoët.

more.problem: Patients with right-ventricular outflow tract dysfunction need a valve implanted by catheter; landing-zone size and coronary compression are hard to judge beforehand. Existing benches replicated geometry well but flow poorly, took long to set up and leaked.
approach: Pipeline from patient CT/MR to segmentation and a 3D-printed model of the outflow tract
Bench replicating the cath-lab procedure: flow inlet and outlet, contrast injection and balloon dilation
Benchmarked against a commercial bench (4–6 min setup, negligible leakage)
New connector and holder design for faster setup and fewer leaks
outcome: A compact PPVI bench concept with lower setup time, plus observation of live procedures to identify clinical needs

headline: A redesigned bench for rehearsing catheter pulmonary valve implantation on 3D-printed, patient-specific outflow tracts, built to set up faster and leak less.

brief.problem: In congenital right-ventricular outflow tract dysfunction, a valve is implanted by catheter. Landing-zone diameter, balloon size, feasibility and the absence of coronary compression are hard to judge beforehand. Available simulation benches reproduce the geometry well but the flow poorly.
brief.built: A review of the image-guided pipeline (CT/MR/angiography, segmentation, 3D model, fusion imaging) and of the current bench: heart and oesophagus holders in a plexiglass tank, ultrasound access, flow inlet and outlet, contrast injection and balloon dilation. Its fixed connectors made set-up slow and leaked. The proposed PPVI bench keeps the materials of the current bench, borrows the compactness of the Biomodex device and improves the connections.
brief.result: A compact bench concept with lower setup time, benchmarked against a commercial bench (4–6 min setup, negligible leakage), plus clinical needs gathered by observing live procedures.

role: Studied the existing congenital-heart simulation bench against the cath-lab procedure, benchmarked a commercial bench, and proposed a PPVI bench concept with a faster set-up and better connections. Presented as an M1 project.
team: M1 BME, École Polytechnique. Advisor Dr Sébastien Hascoët, Hôpital Marie Lannelongue.

name: Soft particles for drug delivery
eli5: Watch tiny soft gel beads squeeze through channels to learn how drug carriers might move in blood.
summary: Experiments on soft gels and particle suspensions as model drug-delivery systems, with Gabriel Amselem and Charles Paul Moore.

more.problem: Drug carriers deform and interact as they flow; soft-gel particles are a controllable model to study that.
approach: Microfluidic experiments with soft gels and particle suspensions
Automated pipeline to track and analyse particles in image sequences, speeding up result synthesis
outcome: Faster, reproducible analysis of experimental videos

headline: Flow experiments on soft gel particles as stand-ins for deformable drug carriers, with an automated pipeline that tracks particles across the recorded image sequences.

brief.problem: Drug carriers deform and interact as they flow. A soft hydrogel microparticle pushed through a constriction is a controllable model, but each test produces long image sequences at several flow rates that are slow to measure by hand.
brief.built: MATLAB tools for the experiments. Image sequences are cleaned with a median image, and circle detection finds the microgels. A line ROI on thresholded images tracks interface displacement, with the frame rate as input. For each microgel tested at several flow rates in the same gap, elongation is measured semi-automatically, PIV gives the flow and hydrodynamic resistance, pressure follows, and the elastic modulus is estimated iteratively as the combined modulus of the microgel and the trap walls.
brief.result: Faster, reproducible analysis of the experimental videos, which sped up the synthesis of results.

role: Wrote MATLAB analysis scripts (the gel-detection and interface-displacement scripts carry his author header): image pre-processing, microgel detection, semi-automated length and interface measurements. The elasticity and resistance script builds on PIVlab.

name: Flexible dry electrodes
eli5: Sticky gel patches are messy; we designed soft, dry electrodes that still read the heart while you move.
summary: Design, fabrication and characterisation of flexible dry electrodes for physiological measurements on the move, for the sleep-monitoring startup Manitty. Team: Sai Kiran Kumar Nalla, Yuhui Wang, Koohyar Habibi.

more.problem: Wet gel electrodes are uncomfortable for long recordings and dry electrodes struggle with skin impedance and motion artefacts.
approach: Design constraints from literature: diameter under 10–20 mm, contact area at least 6 cm², contact impedance 20–40 kΩ, 95–98 % correlation with wet electrodes at rest and 85–90 % in motion, €10–30 per electrode
Fabricated flexible pin electrodes in PDMS with conductive PEDOT:PSS and graphite, plus 3D-printed variants
Mechanical characterisation by atomic force microscopy (surface and Young's modulus), then electrical characterisation in vitro
outcome: Electrode designs evaluated against the constraints, with options for human and veterinary use

headline: Gel-free, flexible pin electrodes in PDMS with PEDOT:PSS and graphite, designed for the sleep-monitoring startup Manitty to record while the wearer moves.

brief.problem: Wet gel electrodes are uncomfortable over long recordings, and dry electrodes struggle with the skin's stratum corneum (10–20 µm), skin impedance and motion artefacts. Hair adds to the pin length needed on animals.
brief.built: Targets from the literature: contact diameter under 10–20 mm, at least 6 cm² of skin contact, 20–40 kΩ contact impedance, 4–6 h of fabrication, 1–2 years of use, EUR 10–30 per electrode, and 95–98 % correlation with wet electrodes at rest (85–90 % in motion). Flexible pin electrodes were moulded in PDMS with PEDOT:PSS and graphite, alongside 3D-printed, silver-coated and composite versions.
brief.result: AFM gave average Young's moduli of 2.3 MPa (PDMS base) to 4.8 MPa (PDMS pins), and 3.9 to 4.5 MPa with graphite. Impedance spectroscopy on the first prototypes pointed to a capacitance problem. The prototypes were then scored against the constraints in a design evaluation.

role: Team project: literature review and design constraints, mould trials, PDMS and PEDOT:PSS pin electrodes, 3D-printed and coated variants, mechanical characterisation by atomic force microscopy and electrical impedance spectroscopy, and a final design evaluation.
team: Sai Kiran Kumar Nalla, Yuhui Wang and Koohyar Habibi (Master BME, École Polytechnique) with Manitty, a start-up building human and veterinary sensors.

name: Shear encapsulation into red blood cells
eli5: Squeeze red blood cells just enough that medicine slips inside, but not so much that they break.
summary: Modelling of shear-induced membrane poration and drug diffusion to load particles into red blood cells in microchannel flow, compared with experiments. With Camille Awade.

more.problem: Encapsulation needs enough shear to open membrane pores and enough time for drugs to diffuse in, but too much shear destroys the cell (haemolysis).
approach: Modelled RBC mechanics, shear-induced poration and diffusion through the cytoplasm
Computational results compared with published microfluidic experiments
outcome: About 30 % average encapsulation with around 80 % of cells preserved in the worst cases
Open issues: physiological haematocrit (~40 %), pulsatile flow, biocompatibility and circulation time

headline: A model of loading drugs into red blood cells with shear flow: about 30 % average encapsulation while around 80 % of cells survive in the worst cases.

brief.problem: Shear can open transient pores in red blood cell membranes so a drug can diffuse in, but too much shear or exposure damages the cell. RBCs last about 120 days in circulation and make up 45 % of blood volume, which makes them attractive carriers.
brief.built: An analysis of four studies (Piergiovanni 2019 on encapsulation, Rahman 2021 on controlled shear deformation, Wu 2015 and Jung & Hassanein 2008 on blood-flow models). The two-fluid (Euler-Euler) and mixture models, with the drag, lift and viscosity closures, were compared with the experiments through a normalised encapsulation index built from velocity, shear stress and cell volume fraction.
brief.result: The model's best encapsulation index is 0.36 (about 36 %), against 22.4 ± 19.0 % (men) and 21.8 ± 13.3 % (women) measured, and 25 ± 5 % of human cells in the second study. Optimal shear was about 80 Pa in the model and 83.44 Pa measured, in the sub-hemolytic zone. About 30 % average encapsulation with around 80 % of cells preserved in the worst cases. Open issues: haematocrit of 1–5 % versus about 40 % in vivo, pulsatile flow, biocompatibility and circulation time.

role: Co-authored the report and slides: compared the computational models (Euler-Euler and mixture) with the two experimental encapsulation studies, and set out the open issues.
team: Camille Awade and Sai Kiran Kumar Nalla. MEC 550 Biofluid Mechanics and Mass Transport, École Polytechnique (Prof. Barakat, 2021).

name: Gas embolism in the carotid artery
eli5: What happens when an air bubble gets into the artery feeding the brain? We simulated it.
summary: Computational study of how gas emboli change pulsatile blood flow in a human carotid artery, supervised by Sebastian Uppapalli; published in the Journal of Biomechanical Engineering (2022).
abstract:
Atherosclerosis in carotid arteries depends mostly on hemodynamic parameters, and any disturbances in pulsatile flows may alter the hemodynamic parameters extensively. Gas emboli are one such source that can hinder and disturb standard blood flow patterns and potentially lead to occlusions and ischemia. To understand how gas embolism affects carotid artery hemodynamics, numerical simulation of coupled Newtonian two-phase laminar flow with interface tracking are performed in an anatomical image-based geometry with flow conditions closely approximating physiological flows. Bubble behavior and Pulsatile flow field changes are quantified. Significant deviation from flow without gas embolism is observed leading to nonstandard flow distributions.

Results: show that gas embolism promotes complex spatio-temporal variations in the carotid artery hemodynamics leading to higher time averaged shear stress values and greater regions of high oscillatory shear index, implying higher probability of atherosclerosis incidence. Depending on contact angle, gas emboli were found to be lodged in carotid sinus or exiting the carotid artery, which can potentially cause abnormalities in blood pressures, heart rates, and ischemia in downstream vasculature, respectively.
headline: Two-phase CFD of a gas bubble travelling through an image-based human carotid artery under pulsatile flow, published in the Journal of Biomechanical Engineering (2022).

brief.problem: Gas emboli (surgery, lung trauma, blast injury) can block arteries; in the carotid they threaten the brain. Single-phase CFD of the carotid is well studied, but gas embolism in an image-based carotid geometry with a bifurcation had not been simulated.
brief.built: Coupled Newtonian two-phase laminar simulations with the level-set method (Navier-Stokes with interfacial tension and contact angle) in an MRI-based carotid with a bubble placed in the common carotid. Inlet flow rate and outlet pressure waveforms at 60 bpm give pulsatile flow. The single-phase model was checked against the known carotid flow pattern (about 69 % of inflow to the ICA, sinus vortex), and the two-phase model against microfluidic T-junction droplet experiments.
brief.result: The bubble creates transverse pressure gradients in the common carotid and changes the recirculation zone in the sinus. This gives lower, oscillating wall shear stress and more regions prone to atherosclerosis. At small contact angles the bubble is trapped in the carotid sinus, where it could disturb blood-pressure control; at large angles it leaves the artery. Bubble size mattered only when it touched the wall. Published in J Biomech Eng 2022.

role: First author of the paper (corresponding author: Sebastian Uppapalli), written during the research associate post at Mahindra University.
team: Nalla Sai Kiran Kumar and Sebastian Uppapalli, École Centrale School of Engineering, Mahindra University (research associate, 2020–2021).
